article_text:
Al Museo Civico Archeologico di Bologna è possibile visitare la mostra Elliott Erwitt. L’arte di osservare, curata da Biba Giacchetti – collaboratrice storica di Elliot Erwitt – prodotta da Civita Mostre e Musei in collaborazione con il Settore Musei Civici di Bologna.

È la stessa curatrice a definire l’esposizione non come una semplice retrospettiva, bensì come un «ritratto in movimento». Ciò che da essa affiora è, infatti, la delineazione della trama artistica e umana di un autore capace di muoversi tra sfera pubblica e privata, alternando vita quotidiana a episodi che hanno segnato il Novecento. È in questo continuo passaggio di registro che risiede la singolarità assoluta di Elliot Erwitt: la capacità di mostrare quanto sia labile tale confine, declinato attraverso la sua «arte di osservare».

L’arte di osservare dell’autore appare come delicata e mai invadente, concede allo spettatore il permesso di accedere in modo silenzioso alle differenti situazioni umane: da ritratto della piccola Ellen sul letto, allo storico incontro tra Nikita Khrushchev and Richard Nixon , fino al famoso scatto Matrimonio di Bratsk . La retrospettiva si configura così come un dialogo coerente e armonioso, nel quale le diverse fotografie confluiscono in un unico racconto, dimostrando come i grandi eventi storici e momenti privati siano indissolubilmente legati dallo stesso filo umano.

Una delle fotografie esposte che incarna perfettamente questa poetica è USA, North Carolina, Segregated Water Fountains , scatto diventato simbolo della segregazione razziale negli Stati Uniti tra gli anni Cinquanta e Sessanta del Novecento. L’immagine ritrae un uomo afroamericano intento a bere da un lavello fatiscente, collocato al fianco di una ben più curata fontanella. Sulla parete, le due diciture emblematiche – white e colored – trasformano la fotografia in una testimonianza di un’umanità frammentata dal pregiudizio e prigioniera di assurdi condizionamenti sociali.

Il percorso espositivo, contenente circa cento scatti, si articola in cinque sezioni. Alle immagini che hanno consacrato la fama internazionale del fotografo – dal bacio nello specchietto retrovisore alle fotografie dei grandi della terra – si affiancano fotografie appartenenti alla sua collezione privata, con l’introduzione di alcuni scatti inediti esposti per la prima volta. È interessante, quindi, come all’Elliott Erwitt più noto e amato si accosti una dimensione meno conosciuta della sua produzione, che ne rivela il lato più intimo.

Il fil rouge che attraversa e unifica l’intero progetto è la sua inconfondibile vena ironica. L’ironia di Erwitt si caratterizza per una profonda matrice empatica, in grado di portare alla luce la fragilità, le assurdità e la bellezza intrinseca dell’esistenza. L’intento non è mai derisorio, quanto piuttosto di partecipazione: un modo per rimarcare la comune vulnerabilità dell’essere umano, magnifico nella propria ineludibile e talvolta persino divertente inadeguatezza. La sua ironia, unitamente al già citato intreccio tra la sfera pubblica e quella privata, pervade l’intera mostra: dalla sezione dedicata alle immagini personali, a quella dedicata proprio all’ironia, fino ai ritratti dei cani e alla serie conclusiva degli autoritratti.

All’origine di questa visiona c’è la biografia di uomo autenticamente cosmopolita. Nato nella capitale francese da una famiglia russa emigrata all’indomani della Rivoluzione, cresciuto a Milano e in seguito costretto a fuggire negli Stati Uniti a causa dell’introduzione delle leggi razziali. Pur avendo vissuto gli anni dell’adolescenza in sostanziale solitudine, non ha mai maturato sentimenti di rivalsa, mantenendo un legame d’affetto speciale con l’Italia, paese in cui è ritornato a più riprese. Proprio la relazione con l’Italia è oggetto di un’attenzione particolare all’interno dell’esposizione. Il Paese non viene rappresentato come un semplice contesto scenografico, ma si configura come un terreno di esplorazione e di sperimentazione visiva ed emotiva, come testimoniano le opere in mostra, scattate prevalentemente nella Roma degli anni Cinquanta e in altre località del Paese.

Il percorso espositivo offre così un accesso intimo e inedito sull’universo artistico e personale di Elliott Erwitt. Capace di cogliere con la stessa sensibilità sia la drammaticità degli eventi sia l’ironia della vita quotidiana, il fotografo fonde l’immediatezza dell’intuizione visiva con una profonda riflessione concettuale. È proprio nel perfetto equilibrio tra questi aspetti, solo apparentemente opposti, che si racchiude l’essenza della sua poetica.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Penélope Cruz had been a muse to Los Javis — the moniker for Spanish filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo — for years before they met for lunch to persuade her to play a singer (more a force of nature, really) in La Bola Negra , an electrifying sensation at Cannes that’s now Spain’s entry for best international feature film Oscar .", "links": [{"text": "Penélope Cruz", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/penelope-cruz-2/"}, {"text": "Los Javis", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/los-javis/"}, {"text": "La Bola Negra", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/la-bola-negra/"}, {"text": "Spain’s entry for best international feature film Oscar", "url": "https://deadline.com/lists/oscars-2027-international-feature-film-submissions/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I saw her in a clip of Jamón Jamón ,” says Ambrossi, referring to Bigas Luna’s 1992 picture, in which Cruz appeared for the first time opposite her now-husband Javier Bardem. “I was young, and I thought, ‘Who is she ?!’ ”"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Related Stories"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/200723.jpg?w=300", "alt": "‘La Bola Negra’", "caption": "", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "‘La Bola Negra’ Review: Spain’s Javier Calvo And Javier Ambrossi Capture Hearts With Their Unashamedly Romantic Decades-Spanning Drama – Cannes Film Festival", "links": [{"text": "‘La Bola Negra’ Review: Spain’s Javier Calvo And Javier Ambrossi Capture Hearts With Their Unashamedly Romantic Decades-Spanning Drama – Cannes Film Festival", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/05/la-bola-negra-review-javier-calvo-and-javier-ambrossi-penelope-cruz-1236918715/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/La-Bola-Negra-Cannes.jpg?w=300", "alt": "CANNES, FRANCE - MAY 21: (L-R) Javier Calvó, Javier Ambrossi and Penélope Cruz depart the \"La Bola Negra\" screening during the 79th annual Cannes Film Festival at Palais des Festivals on May 21, 2026 in Cannes, France. (Photo by Kate Green/Getty Images)", "caption": "", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Penélope Cruz’s ‘La Bola Negra’ Lands 20-Minute Ovation From Overjoyed Audience At Cannes", "links": [{"text": "Penélope Cruz’s ‘La Bola Negra’ Lands 20-Minute Ovation From Overjoyed Audience At Cannes", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/05/la-bola-negra-cannes-ovation-penelope-cruz-1236917575/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Calvo was similarly enchanted when he saw Cruz in Pedro Almodóvar’s 1999 Oscar winner All About My Mother . “She’s got that material of the stars,” he says. “When you put a camera in front of her, she can do anything, and she doesn’t even realize what she’s doing. There’s a power , there’s a force guiding her, and that’s amazing to see first-hand.”"}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Watch on Deadline"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Los Javis wanted Cruz for a small but pivotal role in their epic tale La Bola Negra , the intertwined story of three gay men who exist in three different time periods in Spain. In 1932, Carlos (Milo Quifes) is a young man in Grenada at a time when Spain is lurching uncomfortably towards an ever-increasing spiteful intolerance of homosexuality. In 1937, against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War, Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) and Rafael ( Miguel Bernardeau ) are soldiers from opposing political divides brought closer by the conflict. And in 2017, Alberto (Carlos González) is a playwright from Madrid who engages with an eminent Federico Garcia Lorca scholar (played by another Hollywood star, Glenn Close , speaking fluent Spanish) in a storyline that links the characters in the prior timelines.", "links": [{"text": "Miguel Bernardeau", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/miguel-bernardeau/"}, {"text": "Glenn Close", "url": "https://deadline.com/tag/glenn-close/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "RELATED: Netflix Unveils U.S. Market Rollout For ‘La Bola Negra’ Theatrical Release", "links": [{"text": "Netflix Unveils U.S. Market Rollout For ‘La Bola Negra’ Theatrical Release", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/09/netflix-la-bola-negra-markets-box-office-1237073639/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Cruz’s character, one Nené Romero, performs for the troops in a series of beautifully choreographed, risqué numbers that the boys, far from home, lap up with hunger in their eyes. Los Javis say that Nené was inspired by La Fornarina, a cupletista , a Spanish singer of cuplé songs — bawdy numbers about “sex and drugs,” as Calvo explains it — who performed in theaters in Madrid around the turn of the last century."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Their research included the study of the erotic novels penned by Spanish writer and fashion designer Álvaro Retana, who also wrote lyrics for saucy songs of the type that Cruz performs in La Bola Negra . “They would be singing all over Madrid. They were so funny, they were unleashed — and they thought they were going to be free forever,” says Calvo when we meet in a suite at the swanky Corinthia Hotel during the London Film Festival. “But these singers and their gay friends, all the people in that circle, they were all incarcerated, persecuted, killed or disappeared. They’re forgotten, kind of. So we wanted to bring them back.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Cruz was already a fan of Los Javis having been gripped by their outrageously captivating 2023 TV drama miniseries La Mesías , a hit for Moviestar+ in Spain, which is now available via Mubi in the UK, Canada Turkey, the Netherlands, Germany and Australia, and will soon be streaming in France. “They are so talented,” I recall an ecstatic Cruz telling me at the closing-night party in Cannes. “I saw their first television show Veneno as well,” she said, “and now they’ve won the directing prize at Cannes .”", "links": [{"text": "won the directing prize at Cannes", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/05/cannes-2026-winners-live-updating-1236919837/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The next time they work with Cruz, says Ambrossi, they plan to create “a whole film around her,” but that will be be after what they hope will be their next feature project, a movie that they claim will be “90% in English.” That movie, whenever it’s made, will likely have a larger budget than Los Javis spent on La Bola Negra . Ambrossi says that its roughly $15 million budget was tight but it’s “big for a Spanish movie.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://deadline.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/La-Bola-Negra_Group00841.jpg?w=300", "alt": "The 'La Bola Negra’ team at TIFF ", "caption": "The ‘La Bola Negra’ team at the Deadline Studio during the Toronto Film Festival Deadline", "credit": "Deadline · Film"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "With time and the right people on La Bola Negra , Ambrossi adds, “we knew we could do it big. The scope is not always about big landscapes; it’s about how you position people, so you get the sense that it’s bigger, and taking the time to find the right locations, because these are all natural locations.“ They also insisted on making time for proper rehearsals before the 12-week shoot (“Because it’s a deep story and the actors needed time”)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Calvo explains that with the purse strings being so tight they had to find “creative solutions.” They didn’t, for example, have a room in which to shoot all the soldiers having dinner. “We’re like, “OK, then we’ll compose a beautiful shot with everyone outside with tables, and we’ll just imagine they went out to have dinner there,” he explains."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "They also turned to “the godfathers of cinema,” as Calvo refers to such legendary directors as Thodōros Angelopoulos ( Alexander the Great ) and Andrei Tarkovsky ( Solaris ), who, “with just with a landscape, mist and composing the humans in a proper way” were able to conjure up scenes of movie magic."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Working with the sublime cinematographer Gris Jordana — a frequent collaborator, as are the film’s editor, production designer, hair and makeup designer, costume designer, composer, and many other key creatives — Los Javis sought to bring some of that “godfathers of cinema” magic to their own film. “They’re part of our team,” Amborossi says. “We have been growing together. In every project we learn together. So that’s why the movie is so big, even if the budget is not. They put a lot of effort because it’s a collective experience. It’s like they put in their souls.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“This is a movie about poetry,” says Calvo, “and there’s also a poetry in images. You don’t have to show everything. You can give something, and the viewer will leave it to their imagination.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "RELATED: ‘La Bola Negra’ Directors Dig Into Generational Trauma: “Something Touched Deep Inside” – Contenders London", "links": [{"text": "‘La Bola Negra’ Directors Dig Into Generational Trauma: “Something Touched Deep Inside” – Contenders London", "url": "https://deadline.com/2026/10/la-bola-negra-generational-trauma-contenders-london-1237151053/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ambrosssi jumps in. “If you don’t have the money, just don’t do it badly,” he says. “Cut it, and someone can talk about it in the next scene. Sometimes we needed a natural beauty location. For example, we didn’t have an office for the general lieutenant featured in the film, so we found an empty space with a nice view — you can see the sea — and we composed it with people and a table and a small framed picture of Franco, and that was it. And that’s not expensive.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The main point, Calvo believes — as the likes of David Lean found while directing Lawrence of Arabia — is that it was necessary to find intimacy within such an epic story."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Los Javis were helped in that endeavor, Calvo adds, because the film is loosely based on Alberto Conejero’s one-act play La Piedra Oscura , which deals only with the relationship between Rafael and Sebastian, a play that is “so intimate and delicate” that they wanted to expand it into a triptych. ”Like, a big movie,” says Calvo, spreading his arms wide, “and an intimate movie at the same time. article_text:
Penélope Cruz had been a muse to Los Javis — the moniker for Spanish filmmakers Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo — for years before they met for lunch to persuade her to play a singer (more a force of nature, really) in La Bola Negra , an electrifying sensation at Cannes that’s now Spain’s entry for best international feature film Oscar .

“I saw her in a clip of Jamón Jamón ,” says Ambrossi, referring to Bigas Luna’s 1992 picture, in which Cruz appeared for the first time opposite her now-husband Javier Bardem. “I was young, and I thought, ‘Who is she ?!’ ”

Related Stories

‘La Bola Negra’ Review: Spain’s Javier Calvo And Javier Ambrossi Capture Hearts With Their Unashamedly Romantic Decades-Spanning Drama – Cannes Film Festival

Penélope Cruz’s ‘La Bola Negra’ Lands 20-Minute Ovation From Overjoyed Audience At Cannes

Calvo was similarly enchanted when he saw Cruz in Pedro Almodóvar’s 1999 Oscar winner All About My Mother . “She’s got that material of the stars,” he says. “When you put a camera in front of her, she can do anything, and she doesn’t even realize what she’s doing. There’s a power , there’s a force guiding her, and that’s amazing to see first-hand.”

Watch on Deadline

Los Javis wanted Cruz for a small but pivotal role in their epic tale La Bola Negra , the intertwined story of three gay men who exist in three different time periods in Spain. In 1932, Carlos (Milo Quifes) is a young man in Grenada at a time when Spain is lurching uncomfortably towards an ever-increasing spiteful intolerance of homosexuality. In 1937, against the backdrop of the Spanish Civil War, Sebastián (Guitarricadelafuente) and Rafael ( Miguel Bernardeau ) are soldiers from opposing political divides brought closer by the conflict. And in 2017, Alberto (Carlos González) is a playwright from Madrid who engages with an eminent Federico Garcia Lorca scholar (played by another Hollywood star, Glenn Close , speaking fluent Spanish) in a storyline that links the characters in the prior timelines.

RELATED: Netflix Unveils U.S. Market Rollout For ‘La Bola Negra’ Theatrical Release

Cruz’s character, one Nené Romero, performs for the troops in a series of beautifully choreographed, risqué numbers that the boys, far from home, lap up with hunger in their eyes. Los Javis say that Nené was inspired by La Fornarina, a cupletista , a Spanish singer of cuplé songs — bawdy numbers about “sex and drugs,” as Calvo explains it — who performed in theaters in Madrid around the turn of the last century.

Their research included the study of the erotic novels penned by Spanish writer and fashion designer Álvaro Retana, who also wrote lyrics for saucy songs of the type that Cruz performs in La Bola Negra . “They would be singing all over Madrid. They were so funny, they were unleashed — and they thought they were going to be free forever,” says Calvo when we meet in a suite at the swanky Corinthia Hotel during the London Film Festival. “But these singers and their gay friends, all the people in that circle, they were all incarcerated, persecuted, killed or disappeared. They’re forgotten, kind of. So we wanted to bring them back.”

Cruz was already a fan of Los Javis having been gripped by their outrageously captivating 2023 TV drama miniseries La Mesías , a hit for Moviestar+ in Spain, which is now available via Mubi in the UK, Canada Turkey, the Netherlands, Germany and Australia, and will soon be streaming in France. “They are so talented,” I recall an ecstatic Cruz telling me at the closing-night party in Cannes. “I saw their first television show Veneno as well,” she said, “and now they’ve won the directing prize at Cannes .”

The next time they work with Cruz, says Ambrossi, they plan to create “a whole film around her,” but that will be be after what they hope will be their next feature project, a movie that they claim will be “90% in English.” That movie, whenever it’s made, will likely have a larger budget than Los Javis spent on La Bola Negra . Ambrossi says that its roughly $15 million budget was tight but it’s “big for a Spanish movie.”

With time and the right people on La Bola Negra , Ambrossi adds, “we knew we could do it big. The scope is not always about big landscapes; it’s about how you position people, so you get the sense that it’s bigger, and taking the time to find the right locations, because these are all natural locations.“ They also insisted on making time for proper rehearsals before the 12-week shoot (“Because it’s a deep story and the actors needed time”).

Calvo explains that with the purse strings being so tight they had to find “creative solutions.” They didn’t, for example, have a room in which to shoot all the soldiers having dinner. “We’re like, “OK, then we’ll compose a beautiful shot with everyone outside with tables, and we’ll just imagine they went out to have dinner there,” he explains.

They also turned to “the godfathers of cinema,” as Calvo refers to such legendary directors as Thodōros Angelopoulos ( Alexander the Great ) and Andrei Tarkovsky ( Solaris ), who, “with just with a landscape, mist and composing the humans in a proper way” were able to conjure up scenes of movie magic.

Working with the sublime cinematographer Gris Jordana — a frequent collaborator, as are the film’s editor, production designer, hair and makeup designer, costume designer, composer, and many other key creatives — Los Javis sought to bring some of that “godfathers of cinema” magic to their own film. “They’re part of our team,” Amborossi says. “We have been growing together. In every project we learn together. So that’s why the movie is so big, even if the budget is not. They put a lot of effort because it’s a collective experience. It’s like they put in their souls.”

“This is a movie about poetry,” says Calvo, “and there’s also a poetry in images. You don’t have to show everything. You can give something, and the viewer will leave it to their imagination.”

RELATED: ‘La Bola Negra’ Directors Dig Into Generational Trauma: “Something Touched Deep Inside” – Contenders London

Ambrosssi jumps in. “If you don’t have the money, just don’t do it badly,” he says. “Cut it, and someone can talk about it in the next scene. Sometimes we needed a natural beauty location. For example, we didn’t have an office for the general lieutenant featured in the film, so we found an empty space with a nice view — you can see the sea — and we composed it with people and a table and a small framed picture of Franco, and that was it. And that’s not expensive.”

The main point, Calvo believes — as the likes of David Lean found while directing Lawrence of Arabia — is that it was necessary to find intimacy within such an epic story.

Los Javis were helped in that endeavor, Calvo adds, because the film is loosely based on Alberto Conejero’s one-act play La Piedra Oscura , which deals only with the relationship between Rafael and Sebastian, a play that is “so intimate and delicate” that they wanted to expand it into a triptych. ”Like, a big movie,” says Calvo, spreading his arms wide, “and an intimate movie at the same time. You have the fragility and the the war, so it’s about contrast. And it was so nice to create that, because sometimes it’s more difficult to create the relationship of Rafael and Sebastian, with all the tension, than a bombing scene.”

Countless meetings with key creatives were held in pre-production to map out the movie, and the more mistakes they made the better, because it meant they’d go out and get it right during the shoot, says Ambrossi. “It’s like, work, work, work, work, make a mistake, then try again,” he says, smiling. The work, however, didn’t feel like work. ”I always go back and say, ‘Oh, wow, it was the journey of our lives,’” Calvo declares.

RELATED: Netflix Enters Box Office Era With ‘La Bola Negra’; ‘You Can See Everything’ & ‘Musk’ Face Off – Specialty Preview

Ambrossi contends that the film is proudly gay, whether that puts it in a niche box or not; it’s “a gay movie” and “I love to keep it that way,” he says. “I want people to have an experience that is universal. But I don’t want them to miss that it’s gay.”

It’s certainly unusual to see a gay story against the backdrop of war. Calvo cites Tarkovsky’s classic Ivan’s Childhood , Elem Klimov’s harrowing Come and See and Francis Ford Coppola’s Apocalypse Now as being amongst his favorite war movies. “So, I have those references,” he says, “but my emotion is another thing, and my sensitivity is what we’re portraying. Why shouldn’t I make a movie the same way the people that made war movies I admire made, but telling my own story and using my own feelings? For me, it was natural to just talk about myself through my references. And why can’t we have it all?”

Ambrossi laughs. “It’s great that we told everyone it is a gay film with — mostly — gay actors portraying gay characters, directed by gay people about the queer experience, and it’s hitting the No. 1 spot at the box office every single night in Spain. I like that. I think it’s cool, because it really represents two things; one, that the world is going in a direction that we are not always aware, and also that the industry has to understand that gay stories are not niche.”

La Bola Negra is a starting point for the next conversation, Ambrosssi continues, and that “once we try, once we prove them wrong, then we can have the conversation about universal stories. But we had to tell them, ‘You don’t have to change the lead and put a straight star in it to get the audience.’ They just go, “Ah, it’s a gay story.’”

Were they pressured in any way to compromise? “They don’t even try to do it with us, because we write, direct and produce. It’s our movie,” Ambrossi responds with gusto. He allows, however, that they encountered difficulties making the 2020 miniseries Veneno . “It was a show with trans actresses, and everyone was like, ‘You won’t find that many trans actresses to put in a show in Spain.’ And we were like, ‘We’ll do it.’ And we did.”

RELATED: ‘La Bola Negra’s Los Javis On Completing The Final Work Of Gay Poet “Murdered By Fascism” In 1936 Spain — Toronto Studio

During their travels promoting the movie — at Cannes (where Los Javis shared the best director prize with Fatherland’s Pawel Pawlikowski), Telluride, Toronto (where it won the People’s Choice Award for best film), San Sebastián (where the film was honored with the festival’s Audience Award) and here in London — the reaction has been overwhelmingly positive. “The feedback from non-gay people, non-LGBTQ people, is the same. This idea of wanting to be yourself, being rejected, a lot of women get that. It gets everyone. At some point, it’s about family, about motherhood, about brotherhood, about friendship. It’s a war movie. It’s about being different, but it’s about art and the power of art.”

Calvo, listening intently, jumps in, pointing out that the film is “about understanding and seeing the other as a human being. Which is, I think, important.”

xxx

When it came to casting the male leads, they chose singer-musician Guitarricadelafuente because they were drawn to the “magnetism, the sadness” in his eyes. “He had to be the eyes of the viewer,” says Calvo, “and he has eyes that you can rely on, and he had this shyness, but also this bravery, this strength, but then this subtleness. We just knew it was for him.”

Ambrossi, meanwhile, hails Bernardeau ( Elite ) as being “one of the best of his generation.” “We needed his technique,” he explains, “because Guitarricadelafuente is new, so we needed the balance to play off each other.” The same goes for González. “He’s so flamboyant and fun in real life,” Ambrossi says. “Here, he’s doing a job that you cannot imagine. If you were to meet him, you would be like, ‘Are you the same person ?’”

Indeed, I spoke with González at a soirée following a special screening of La Bola Negra at Tate Modern, and he was an absolute hoot. He vowed to do anything for the film “with its big black balls.” My eyes widened at that remark and our dirty laughter nearly got us turned outta the party.

As for Carlos, they were looking for Andalusian guys, and the moment they saw Quifes’ audition, they shut down the search.

The roles played by Guitarricadelafuente and Bernardeau are the heart of the film, providing its most tender, heartfelt moments. They met for the first time at rehearsals, where Guitarricadelfuente, who’d never acted before, says he felt “100 percent safe” because he was working opposite a professional actor. “It was a very special moment meeting Miguel,” he says.

Having someone like Miguel “really helped me out in this in this journey,” Guitarricadelafuente says. “There was something very special about the way that our characters grew up together, and the development of that intimacy, that way of nonverbal communication, those gestures that communicated so much. I’m grateful for the time that we spent at that room rehearsing.”

Los Javis were “democratic with us,” he notes, because “they let us express ourselves freely, and if there was maybe sometimes in the dialogue something that maybe didn’t resound that much in ourselves, they would say, ‘What would you say? What would you do?’ They let us roll on and magical things happened.”

Were they able to improvise? Bernardeau shakes his head and notes that it wasn’t so much improvisation because of how much thought went into every scene, what with how the three stories intertwine. “You need to be careful with what you change. There’s a lot of detail, so you cannot improvise. But they were very free with us in changing smaller stuff. I did feel very free to try different ways and paths into the scenes.”

I remember covering the film’s ecstatic 20-minute ovation at Cannes in the Grand Théâtre Lumière and watching the faces of this new generation of filmmakers and actors. Bernardeau was holding back tears. “I knew that once I start crying I would not stop,” he admits.

In front of him, he recalls, was the festival’s camera team “and Tilda Swinton clapping and looking at us.” Swinton introduced Bernardeau to her agent Christian Hodell, chief executive of Hamilton Hodell, who now represents him. Now the actor will soon be moving from Spain to live in London.

Guitarricadelafuente remembers looking up to the Lumière’s second tier to see so many young people who’d clearly connected with the film: “That made me feel as if we were at a concert.” He notes that he’s been astonished by how audiences in Spain have flocked to see the picture. Los Javis were known to young people, he says. “Like, there are people in my family that haven’t been to the cinema in 10 years. They feel like they’re missing out on something, because there’s been like a consensus between everybody to see it. It’s not a film about civil war, it’s not a film about Lorca. It’s is a film about life.”

It sure is.

Culturally, Spain’s on a roll. Singer-songwriter Rosalía took the International Artist of the Year at the Brit Awards; La Bola Negra won a major prize at Cannes; and, of course, Spain won the World Cup. Calvo beams a full-wattage smile. “We’re just getting out there.”

Netflix releases the film in theaters Friday in New York City and Los Angeles ahead of a wider release over coming weeks before debuting on streaming in the U.S. and Canada on December 2. Altitude opens the film in the UK on November 6.

article_text:
Cannes 2026 is in full swing and the Film Comment crew is on the ground, cutting through the noise with dispatches, interviews, Podcasts, a special Cannes Critics’ Grid, and much more. This year’s edition is packed with highly anticipated premieres from Ryûsuke Hamaguchi, Valeska Grisebach, James Gray, Paweł Pawlikowski, and many more acclaimed filmmakers.

For our sixth Podcast from the sun-dappled shores of the French Riviera, Sight and Sound’ s Isabel Stevens and scholar Neta Alexander join FC Editor Devika Girish to share their responses to two Competition titles that are sure to generate lots of chatter: Cristian Mungiu’s legal thriller Fjord (3:15) and Pedro Almodóvar’s self-reflexive drama Bitter Christmas (19:25). Next, they turn to two highlights from the festival’s other sections: Austrian director Sandra Wollner’s Everytime (26:00), which premiered as part of Un Certain Regard, and Chilean filmmaker Dominga Sotomayor’s La perra (32:50), a selection in the Directors’ Fortnight program.

Subscribe today to Film Comment to stay up-to-date with all of our Cannes 2026 coverage.

article_text:
10. The Double (2013)

A doppelganger role can be a trap for an actor: either the two roles are not sufficiently distinct, or they are too hammily different, and either way the result can look like a film school graduation project. But Jesse Eisenberg gives a stylish split-personality turn in Richard Ayoade’s adaptation of the Dostoevsky novella. He plays Simon, a nerdily shy and self-effacing computer programmer in a grim futureworld, ignored by his employers and by co-worker Hannah (Mia Wasikowska), with whom he is hopelessly in love. But then his carbon copy, James, arrives, also of course played by Eisenberg. James is a confident alpha-achiever who impresses his bosses and entrances Hannah – to Simon’s gibbering despair.

9. The Squid and the Whale (2005)

Noah Baumbach ’s brutally black-comic movie, based on his own parents’ unhappy relationship, features Eisenberg as the 16-year-old Walt, an unbearably precocious and self-important young man who has inherited all of his father’s pompous mannerisms. His dad is Jeff Daniels, a failed novelist and creative writing professor who enviously fell out with his wife, Walt’s mother (Laura Linney), when her own writing career took off. As Walt leaves the world of childhood behind, this becomes a rare unsympathetic performance for Eisenberg in many ways, and the nerdy mannerisms for which he became famous look spiky, high-handed and charmless – yet the poignant vulnerability is clear enough.

8. Roger Dodger (2002)

This was the teenage Eisenberg’s feature film acting debut, in which his persona of nerdiness, inexperience and bewilderment first arrived in the cinema, along with that patina of self-awareness with which all these things seemed nonetheless to be coated. He is the high school kid Nick, appalled by his own virginity and in dire need of advice on how to make it with girls. He approaches his Lothario uncle Roger – a glorious performance from Campbell Scott – who has just been dumped by his own girlfriend, and, in a frenzy of misogynist rage, Roger takes Nick on a tour of Manhattan’s pickup joints. Eisenberg’s innocence has a charm and openness that Nick’s womaniser lacks. In some ways, he is the opposite of his character in The Squid and the Whale.

7. Adventureland (2009)

Another of the “virgin” performances with which the younger Eisenberg made his name in the indie-adjacent cinema of the 00s, and he cleverly portrays the way in which the lack of sexual experience becomes the very centre of his character’s existence. It’s a coming-of-age story about a guy called James who has gone through a prestigious undergraduate career at college; the world, supposedly, is now his oyster. But he is still a virgin. And to earn cash for grad school he has to take a job in a scuzzy amusement park, ironically or perhaps not ironically called Adventureland, which is to provide education of a different sort and where he falls for his fellow employee, played by Kristen Stewart .

6. Sasquatch Sunset (2024)

It is a film and a role that would challenge any actor: Eisenberg, in full makeup and hairy costume, plays a grunting, nonverbal sasquatch loping through the empty northern California wilderness. He is one of four apelike bigfoot figures who are perhaps the only creatures left alive after some human-made apocalypse, or perhaps we have simply been allowed to share these creatures’ habitual seclusion, their secret existence away from humans. Eisenberg is, perhaps inevitably, the beta-male sasquatch who is less demonstrative than the alpha male grunter. It is a cult performance in a cult film.

5. Café Society (2016)

It was probably Eisenberg’s destiny to work with Woody Allen at some stage – he is in Café Society and, less prominently, in To Rome With Love, from 2012. Café Society is one of Allen’s innumerable light jeux d’ésprit comedies and perhaps not too memorable, but it has a very interesting performance from Eisenberg. He plays a nervy, gauche romantic who is, of course, ventriloquising Allen in the traditional way, but we also see him grow up from boy to man. Set in the US in the 30s, he’s the kid who gets a nepo job in LA as an assistant to his movie-agent uncle and then another in a New York club run by his brother, where he becomes a white-tuxedoed Bogartian figure, nursing a broken heart.

4. Zombieland (2009)

This came out the same year as Adventureland, creating the odd illusion that it was part of some kind of franchise – but no, the two films have nothing to do with each other, although Eisenberg’s appearance in both is not dissimilar; he is, as ever, the shy nerd who is also a potential hottie. (This film was followed up 10 years later by an underpar sequel entitled Zombieland: Double Tap, in which Eisenberg reprised his role.) He plays Columbus, a gauche, brainy guy in a post-apocalyptic landscape infested by zombies. Columbus teams up with Woody Harrelson’s redneck, who is overbearing and moreover keeps ruining his chances of making it with a young woman, played by Emma Stone, who goes on the road with them. His rage with Harrelson results in one of the most entertaining outbursts of Eisenberg’s movie career, as he screams: “You are like a giant, cock-blocking robot developed in some kind of secret government lab!”

3. The Art of Self-Defense (2019)

Film-maker and Brazilian ju-jitsu specialist Riley Stearns created a dark comedy that allowed Eisenberg to explore an interesting possibility to his habitual persona: what if that nerdy, maladroit shyness led not to romcom sexual success, but violence and a general outbreak of toxic masculinity? Eisenberg is Casey, a lonely office worker who is attacked by a gang of bikers and, traumatised, enrols in a karate class. It is led by a charismatic sensei (Alessandro Nivola) whose demands on him become increasingly disturbing.

2. A Real Pain (2024)

This understated, complex, contemporary film is Eisenberg’s directorial masterpiece. He also gives an outstanding performance, all the more interesting in that it is effectively a supporting turn, ceding the spotlight most of the time to Kieran Culkin. (The Polish-set film is also a very personal movie for Eisenberg, who has now taken up Polish citizenship.) Eisenberg plays David, Culkin is his cousin, Benji; the two are on a kind of buddy-movie road trip visit to Poland to visit the childhood home of their late grandmother, who was a Holocaust survivor. Eisenberg plays – inevitably – a strait-laced, uptight figure while Culkin is the more anarchic free spirit, but without the former’s sensibility and maturity, the latter’s performance wouldn’t make sense.

1. The Social Network (2010)

Casting Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg, the young computer genius at Harvard who in 2004 invented Facebook in a frenzy of sexual and social rejection, was a stroke of genius. It allowed Eisenberg to weaponise and make sense of the nerdy onscreen persona that had come so readily to him; it also showed that he was a natural performer of screenwriter Aaron Sorkin’s mile-a-minute dialogue. In Eisenberg’s other films, the underdog-nerd aspect was there as a kind of adorable (or perhaps disquieting) flaw, to be surmounted in the course of the narrative. Here it is the whole point. The nerdiness is the superpower; not getting it on with girls is the equivalent of lifting a car above his head. This was the sensational role which was to get Eisenberg the part of ubervillain Lex Luthor in DC films such as Batman V Superman: Dawn of Justice and Zack Snyder’s Justice League and the smart-alec illusionist J Daniel Atlas in the magician-heist caper Now You See Me. But none of those had anything like the quicksilver brilliance of his Zuckerberg, who is entitled and insufferable, driven and obsessive, always convinced of his intellectual superiority, never conceding any point to anyone in any argument, treating everyone to a nonstop fusillade of putdowns and zingers. Eisenberg convinced a whole generation that this was what Mark Zuckerberg was really like. It is a classic performance.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: It’s been called “beautifully crafted and meticulously composed,” praised by Werner Herzog, awarded at Sundance and honored with five Critics Choice Documentary Awards nominations.

On Wednesday, MUBI released the trailer for Nuisance Bear and announced the theatrical release plan for the documentary directed and filmed by Jack Weisman and Gabriela Osio Vanden : It will open in Los Angeles on November 6 and in New York, Canada and the UK on December 4. Watch the exclusive trailer above.

“For thousands of years, polar bears have migrated along the shores of Hudson Bay in northern Canada,” notes a synopsis. “Today, that ancient rhythm collides with a human world of tourism, surveillance, and control. Nuisance Bear immerses viewers in the experience of a polar bear forced to navigate tourists, wildlife officers, and hunters as climate change delays the freeze and pushes bears closer to human settlements. When a sacred predator is branded a ‘nuisance,’ it becomes unclear who truly belongs in this shared landscape.”

Related Stories

'A Long Winter': Watch First Trailer For Andrew Haigh Drama Starring Fred Hechinger, Ebon Moss-Bachrach, Caitríona Balfe & Kit Connor

New York Times Op-Docs Acquires 'The Revolution Against Death,' Oscar Nominee Joshua Oppenheimer's Film On Quest For Immortality

The filmmakers shot Nuisance Bear in Churchill, Manitoba, which calls itself the “Polar Bear Capital of the World.” “[W]ith striking intimacy and scale, the film observes bears that are constantly monitored, photographed, and redirected,” the synopsis continues. “In tracing this uneasy coexistence, Nuisance Bear becomes a meditation on how humans manage, commodify, and redefine wildlife—overturning the conventions of the nature documentary and reframing animals not as spectacle, but as active agents in a rapidly changing world.”

Watch on Deadline

The film is produced by Jack Weisman, Gabriela Osio Vanden, Will N. Miller, Teddy Leifer, and Michael Code.

“Ultimately, our aim is to collapse the distance between audience and subject,” Weisman and Vanden said in a statement. “By immersing viewers in the bear’s perspective while exposing the human forces shaping every step of its path, we challenge them to see this landscape, both natural and political, as a shared and increasingly contested space. Nuisance Bear invites us to reconsider who truly belongs here and what coexistence demands of all of us.”

Among the many awards for the film are the Grand Jury Prize for U.S. Documentary at the Sundance Film Festival, the 2026 Werner Herzog Film Award, the top prize from the Silk Road International Film Festival in China, and the James Balog Creative Vision Award at Mountainfilm in Telluride, CO. On Tuesday, it was nominated for Best First Documentary Feature, Best Science/Nature Documentary, Best Cinematography and two other awards for the upcoming Critics Choice Documentary Awards.

“From the time we saw the film, we were mesmerized by not only the incredible story of the nuisance bear, but what it says about humanity,” commented Arianna Bocco, Global SVP of Distribution and Acquisitions, MUBI. “The film is beautiful and profound – and we are thrilled to be working with Jack and Gabriela on their stunning feature debut.”

Nuisance Bear is edited by Andres Landau; Cristóbal Tapia De Veer composed the music. Mike Tunalaaq Gibbons narrates the film. Jack Weisman and Gabriela Osio Vanden serve as directors of photography, with additional cinematography by Sam Holling, Michael Code, Ian Kerr, and Jack Gawthrop. Executive producers include Nicole Stott, Emily Osborne, Harry Go, Nicole Quintero Ochoa, Eric Anoee, Joe Karetak, Alex Pritz, Moudhy Al-Rashid, Sam Frohman, Christine D’Souza, Julia Nelson, Adriana Banta, Emily Goldner, ZZ, and Mike Anders.

Watch the Nuisance Bear trailer above.

article_text:
Sette anni, una promessa e una data prestabilita per dirsi addio. In 7 anniversari , opera prima di Sabrina Iannucci , presentata alla Festa del Cinema di Roma 2026 nella sezione Freestyle , l’amore non è una promessa di eternità, ma un’esperienza a termine. Un patto sentimentale che, dietro la leggerezza della commedia romantica, intercetta una delle inquietudini più profonde della Generazione Z, quella di non riuscire più a immaginare il futuro senza esserne spaventati.

Emma, interpretata da Benedetta Porcaroli , lavora con successo come doppiatrice, mentre Teo, a cui presta il volto Lorenzo Zurzolo , è un creativo appassionato di design che si mantiene facendo il rider. Il loro incontro avviene quasi per caso, durante una consegna di hamburger. L’attrazione è immediata, ma dietro l’innamoramento si nascondono fragilità differenti. Emma porta con sé ferite familiari che rendono difficile abbandonarsi ai sentimenti, mentre Teo sembra abitare il mondo con maggiore libertà, opponendosi alle convenzioni e alle aspettative sociali. È lui a proporre una soluzione tanto paradossale quanto rivelatrice. La loro relazione durerà sette anni, trascorsi i quali entrambi saranno liberi di lasciarsi. Stabilire in anticipo la fine significa, per Emma, neutralizzare l’imprevedibilità del dolore. Se l’abbandono è già previsto, non può più cogliere di sorpresa. Il limite diventa così una protezione, una cornice rassicurante entro cui concedersi persino il lusso di amare. La scelta cinematografica racconta molto della condizione giovanile contemporanea. Cresciuta attraversando crisi economiche, instabilità occupazionale e promesse di mobilità sociale sempre più difficili da mantenere, la Generazione Z si confronta con un orizzonte in cui la precarietà non riguarda soltanto il lavoro, ma investe l’identità e le relazioni. Il titolo di studio non garantisce una professione coerente con il percorso compiuto, mentre l’occupazione rischia di trasformarsi in uno strumento di sopravvivenza più che in una possibilità di realizzazione personale. Il lavoro non definisce necessariamente chi si è, perché spesso la priorità consiste nel trovare ciò che permette di restare a galla.

In questo scenario, anche l’intimità viene sottoposta a una forma di controllo preventivo. Progettare una vita insieme significa accettare l’imprevisto, la ripetizione quotidiana, la noia e le inevitabili trasformazioni dell’altro. Meglio, allora, stabilire una scadenza, delimitare il coinvolgimento, ridurre il rischio di perdere il controllo. Ma ciò che nasce per contenere la paura finisce per mettere alla prova proprio la libertà che dovrebbe garantire. Mentre gli anni passano, i sentimenti di Teo ed Emma crescono oltre i confini del patto. Lui spera segretamente che lei cambi idea, mentre la data concordata si avvicina, trasformando il tempo in una presenza costante. Il settimo anniversario non è più soltanto una promessa da mantenere, ma una domanda sul significato stesso dell’amore. Anche la dimensione familiare contribuisce a definire questo paesaggio emotivo. La figura materna richiama un mondo adulto incapace, talvolta, di elaborare le proprie frustrazioni senza trasferirle sui figli, lasciando in eredità paure che continuano a condizionare le relazioni future. Con una sensibilità che conserva tracce della sua esperienza nel cinema documentario, Iannucci, classe 1989, costruisce una commedia dolceamara capace di osservare i sentimenti come fenomeni individuali e, insieme, sociali. Porcaroli e Zurzolo restituiscono con naturalezza le contraddizioni di una coppia che desidera amare senza consegnarsi completamente all’incertezza.

7 anniversari non offre una formula per superare la paura, ma ne individua il paradosso. Nel tentativo di evitare il dolore, Emma e Teo rischiano di sottrarre al presente la sua possibilità più autentica. Per una generazione abituata a considerare ogni certezza provvisoria, forse la sfida non consiste nel promettersi per sempre, ma nell’accettare che nessun legame possa essere vissuto senza esporsi al rischio del cambiamento.
